content.title: About
content.content: Beans and tomatoes with added fat is a ready‑to‑eat product that combines selected beans, a tomato sauce and plant oils. It is designed for quick meal preparation and provides a balanced mix of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Beans are one of the oldest cultivated legumes, grown by humans for over 7,000 years.
Tomatoes are rich in lycopene, which becomes more bioavailable after cooking.
Adding plant fats enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins from tomatoes.
The combination of beans and tomatoes creates a near‑complete amino acid profile, similar to animal protein.
The product is popular in sports nutrition for post‑workout recovery.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: Beans provide about 20 % protein, supporting muscle maintenance and repair.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and helps maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Lycopene and antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes supply lycopene, an antioxidant that protects cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Healthy fats
items.content: The added plant oils aid the absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The product contains iron, magnesium, folate and vitamin C, important for immunity and energy.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Tomato sauces often contain salt; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Legumes can cause bloating in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The product is calorie‑dense; moderate consumption is advised for weight‑controlled diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The product is ready to heat: microwave or simmer on the stove for 3–5 minutes, stir, and serve as a standalone dish, a side for rice or quinoa, or as a filling for wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place at temperatures not exceeding 25 °C. After opening, consume within 5 days or keep refrigerated in an airtight container.

content.title: About
content.content: A cookie raisin sandwich with cream filling is a two‑layer biscuit where a smooth buttery cream is sandwiched between soft cookie shells, with sweet raisins tucked inside. It is enjoyed as a light snack or dessert, offering a pleasant blend of vanilla, butter and dried‑fruit flavors.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first raisin cookie recipes appeared in Europe in the 19th century, while cream‑filled versions became popular in the United States in the early 20th century.
Raisins commonly used are the “Taman” and “Sultan” varieties, known for their bright sweetness and high sugar content.
The cream is typically made from cream cheese, heavy cream and a touch of vanilla extract.
Some versions are finished with a light sugar glaze for a crisp outer crust.
In several countries these sandwiches are served alongside hot tea or coffee.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from the cookies and raisins provide a quick boost of energy, making the product a convenient snack.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Raisins are a good source of iron, which is essential for hemoglobin formation and normal blood function.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Phenolic compounds in raisins help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Calcium from the cream
items.content: The dairy‑based cream supplies calcium, important for bones and teeth.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from raisins aids regular bowel movements.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: The sandwich contains a notable amount of sugar, which may be unsuitable for people with diabetes or those watching their weight.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: The cream often contains milk proteins and lactose, posing a risk for individuals with dairy allergies or intolerance.

items.title: Possible trans fats
items.content: Some commercial versions may use partially hydrogenated oils, which are sources of trans fats.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Because of the combination of cookies, raisins and cream, the product is relatively calorie‑dense; portion control is advised.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the sandwich straight from the package as a snack, include it in lunchboxes, or serve it with tea or coffee. A brief warm‑up in the microwave can make the cream extra soft.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage (over two weeks) refrigerate to maintain cream freshness. Discard any product with off‑odors or altered texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Whole milk is a natural dairy product obtained from cows without removing the fat component. It contains about 3.5 % fat, giving it a creamy texture and characteristic flavor. Milk is consumed fresh, used in cooking, baking, and for preparing beverages.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole milk is rich in calcium, which is essential for bone and tooth health.
It provides all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.
Vitamin D content is often increased by fortification of whole milk.
Milk naturally contains lactase, but people with lactase deficiency may experience discomfort.
Traditionally, whole milk has been used to make cheese, yogurt, and butter.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone density, tooth strength, and is involved in muscle and nerve function.

items.title: High‑quality protein source
items.content: Milk protein contains all essential amino acids, supporting tissue growth and repair.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk provides riboflavin (B2) and B12, which are important for energy metabolism and blood formation.

items.title: Contains mono‑ and polyunsaturated fats
items.content: The fat fraction supplies energy and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

items.title: Phosphorus and potassium
items.content: These minerals help maintain acid‑base balance and support heart function.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People lacking lactase may experience bloating, diarrhea, and discomfort after consuming whole milk.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Allergic reactions can range from skin symptoms to anaphylaxis and require complete avoidance of dairy.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Regular consumption of large amounts of whole milk may raise cholesterol levels in susceptible individuals.

items.title: Pathogen contamination
items.content: Unpasteurized whole milk can contain bacteria such as Salmonella or Listeria, so choosing pasteurized products is important.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Drink whole milk fresh, add it to cereals, smoothies, sauces, baked goods, and use it for desserts. It can be warmed for infant feeding or added to coffee for a smoother taste.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store whole milk in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. After opening, consume within 5‑7 days. Do not freeze, as this can alter the fat structure.

content.title: About
content.content: Ramen bowl with chicken is a ready‑to‑cook kit that includes ramen noodles, seasoned broth, chicken pieces and aromatic spices. Simply pour hot water over the contents, add the chicken, wait a few minutes, and enjoy a flavorful, satisfying Asian‑style meal at home or at the office.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ramen originated in Japan in the early 20th century and quickly became a popular street‑food dish.
Chicken in ramen is often pre‑cooked and sliced thinly to speed up preparation.
Most instant ramen packs use dry seasonings and broth powders that preserve flavor for long periods.
Japan boasts over 10,000 ramen varieties, including chicken, pork, seafood, and vegetarian versions.
Instant ramen noodles are typically made from wheat flour, salt and water, sometimes with added starch for a smoother texture.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: The chicken provides high‑quality protein essential for muscle repair and immune function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Chicken and fortified broth can supply iron, important for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The kit contains B6 and B12 vitamins that support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Carbohydrates for energy
items.content: Ramen noodles deliver quick‑acting carbs that are readily converted into energy.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: The broth often includes sodium, potassium and magnesium, which help maintain fluid and electrolyte balance.

items.title: High sodium
items.content: Instant ramen packets are usually high in salt, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Additives
items.content: Flavor enhancers (MSG), preservatives and artificial aromas may be present and are not suitable for everyone.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Some kits contain gluten, soy sauce or other common allergens.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The dish can be relatively calorie‑rich due to noodles and oil, so portion control is advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour the contents of the packet over hot (not boiling) water, stir, add the chicken pieces and let sit for 3–5 minutes. Optionally garnish with fresh vegetables, herbs, a boiled egg or a splash of soy sauce for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened packets in a dry, cool place away from direct sunlight. After opening, keep the contents in an airtight container to prevent moisture absorption. Follow the expiration date printed on the packaging.

content.title: About
content.content: Scallops are bivalve mollusks from the family Pectinidae. When steamed or boiled they retain a delicate sea flavor, a faint sweetness and a tender yet slightly firm texture. Scallops are commonly served as an appetizer, in salads, soups, or tossed with pasta.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scallops can filter up to 20 liters of water per hour, helping to keep their environment clean.
More than 300 species exist, but the blue mussel (Mytilus edulis) and the great scallop (Pecten maximus) are most widely consumed.
Scallops are capable of changing sex during their life cycle, often starting as males and later becoming females.
In ancient Rome, scallops were considered a delicacy and served at lavish banquets with wine.
Scallops grow quickly; they can increase their biomass five‑ to ten‑fold in a single year.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: Scallops provide about 20 g of protein per 100 g, making them an excellent source of complete animal protein.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: They contain less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, most of which are polyunsaturated fatty acids.

items.title: Rich in vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 supports red blood cell formation and nervous system health; scallops deliver over 100 % of the daily value in a 100‑g serving.

items.title: Contains iron and zinc
items.content: These minerals aid immune function, metabolism, and skin health.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: Scallops provide EPA and DHA, which are beneficial for heart and brain health.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Raw or undercooked scallops may harbor Vibrio bacteria that cause gastroenteritis. Always cook until shells fully open.

items.title: Shellfish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions ranging from hives to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Cholesterol content
items.content: Scallops contain about 50 mg of cholesterol per 100 g, so people with high cholesterol should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Heavy‑metal contamination
items.content: In certain regions scallops can accumulate cadmium or lead; purchase from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steam scallops for 5–7 minutes or boil for 3–4 minutes until the shells open. Serve with lemon, butter‑garlic sauce, or add to risotto, paella, and seafood salads. Discard any scallops whose shells do not open after cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Fresh raw scallops should be kept in the refrigerator (0–2 °C) in a sealed container covered with a damp cloth and used within 24 hours. Frozen scallops retain quality for up to 3 months; thaw them in the refrigerator before cooking.

turkey-light-meat-skin-not-eaten.title: Turkey, light meat, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Turkey is a large bird native to North America. Light turkey meat without skin has a mild flavor, low fat content, and a high amount of protein. It is widely used in dietetic cooking, grilled, roasted, boiled, or stewed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Turkeys were domesticated by Native Americans more than 2,000 years ago.
Light turkey meat contains fewer calories than red meat and is often recommended for weight loss.
Wild turkeys can weigh up to 15 kg, but most commercial birds are 3–5 kg.
Turkey skin is rich in collagen, but skin‑less preparations keep the fat content low.
In the United States turkey is traditionally associated with the Thanksgiving holiday.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Light turkey meat provides about 30 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Without skin, 100 g of turkey contains less than 2 g of fat, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Turkey is high in niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals: selenium and zinc
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant, while zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Low glycemic impact
items.content: Turkey meat does not raise blood‑sugar levels, which is beneficial for people with diabetes.

items.title: Poultry allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to turkey proteins, ranging from skin rashes to anaphylaxis.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw turkey can harbor Salmonella and Campylobacter; it should be cooked to an internal temperature of 74 °C.

items.title: Excess sodium in processed forms
items.content: Smoked or cured turkey products often contain high levels of salt, which can increase blood pressure.

items.title: Additive concerns
items.content: Some commercial turkey items may contain preservatives and flavor enhancers that are unsuitable for people sensitive to food additives.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Light turkey meat without skin can be grilled, roasted, boiled, steamed, or added to salads and soups. It pairs well with herbs (rosemary, thyme), lemon, and spices. Thinly sliced, it works great in sandwiches and wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store fresh turkey in the refrigerator at 0–4 °C for no more than 2 days. Frozen turkey can be kept at –18 °C for up to 9 months. Thaw in the refrigerator, not at room temperature. Keep it in an airtight container to prevent odor transfer.
